paper.title: Ultrasound-guided nerve block and pain after knee surgery

paper_doc.title: Ultrasound-guided nerve block and pain after knee surgery
paper_doc.authors: Oyelaran, D., Voss, H. Department of Anaesthesia and Perioperative Medicine, Fake Regional Teaching Hospital
paper_doc.abstract: Background: Pain in the first day after total knee replacement delays mobilisation and discharge. Peripheral nerve blocks placed under ultrasound guidance may improve early analgesia while sparing motor function. Methods: We conducted a single-centre, randomised, assessor-blinded trial in adults undergoing elective primary total knee replacement under spinal anaesthesia. Patients were allocated to an ultrasound-guided nerve block in addition to standard multimodal analgesia, or to standard multimodal analgesia alone. The primary outcome was pain at rest 24 hours after surgery on an 11-point numerical rating scale. Results: In 160 patients, an ultrasound-guided nerve block lowered pain scores 24 hours after knee replacement. Block-related complications were rare and no falls occurred in either group during the hospital stay. Conclusions: An ultrasound-guided nerve block is a useful addition to multimodal analgesia after knee replacement and may support earlier mobilisation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Total knee replacement is one of the most frequently performed elective operations in adults, and its volume continues to rise as populations age and as surgery is offered to patients with earlier stages of disabling osteoarthritis. Although long-term outcomes are good, the first postoperative day is often marked by moderate to severe pain. Poorly controlled pain at this stage limits participation in physiotherapy, delays the first walk, and is one of the commonest reasons for an unplanned extra night in hospital.
Multimodal analgesia, combining regular paracetamol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug where appropriate, local infiltration by the surgeon, and rescue medication, has become the standard of care in most units. Even so, a substantial proportion of patients report pain that interferes with sleep and movement during the first night. Regional techniques offer a way to target the nerves supplying the knee directly, and a range of blocks has been described, from the femoral nerve block to more distal approaches within the adductor canal.
The femoral nerve block provides reliable analgesia but weakens the quadriceps, and quadriceps weakness has been linked with falls and with slower functional recovery. More distal approaches aim to preserve motor function while covering the sensory branches that matter most for pain after knee surgery. Ultrasound guidance allows the needle and the spread of local anaesthetic to be seen in real time, which may improve the success rate of the block and lower the risk of vascular puncture or nerve injury compared with landmark or nerve stimulator techniques.
Despite wide adoption, the evidence base for ultrasound-guided blocks as an addition to a modern multimodal regimen remains uneven. Many earlier trials compared a block with systemic opioids alone, used regimens no longer typical of current practice, or measured pain only in the first few hours, when the effect of spinal anaesthesia has not yet worn off. Fewer trials have measured pain at 24 hours, the time point at which spinal anaesthesia has resolved, physiotherapy is under way, and decisions about discharge begin to be made.
We therefore designed a pragmatic randomised trial to test whether adding an ultrasound-guided nerve block to standard multimodal analgesia reduces pain 24 hours after primary total knee replacement. We also examined safety, the time to first mobilisation, patient satisfaction and the length of hospital stay.

sections.heading: 2. Methods
sections.text:
2.1 Study design and setting. This was a single-centre, parallel-group, randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment, conducted in the elective orthopaedic unit of a regional teaching hospital. The protocol was approved by the institutional research ethics committee and registered before the first patient was enrolled. All participants gave written informed consent. The trial is reported in line with standard guidance for randomised trials.
2.2 Participants. Adults aged 18 to 85 years scheduled for elective primary unilateral total knee replacement under spinal anaesthesia were eligible. Exclusion criteria were revision surgery, bilateral surgery, known allergy to local anaesthetics, infection at the injection site, pre-existing neuropathy of the operated limb, inability to use the numerical rating scale, and pregnancy. Patients were screened at the preoperative assessment clinic and approached by a member of the research team who was not involved in their clinical care.
2.3 Randomisation and blinding. Allocation was in a 1:1 ratio using computer-generated permuted blocks of variable size, stratified by sex. Allocation was concealed in sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes opened by the anaesthetist in the block room after spinal anaesthesia had been established. Patients in the control group did not receive a sham injection, so patients and the treating anaesthetist were aware of allocation. Outcome assessors, ward nurses recording pain scores for the trial, physiotherapists and the statistician were unaware of group allocation. A small adhesive dressing was placed on the thigh of every patient so that the presence of a block could not be inferred at the bedside.
2.4 Interventions. All patients received spinal anaesthesia with plain bupivacaine, intravenous sedation at the discretion of the anaesthetist, and local infiltration of the joint by the surgeon according to the unit protocol. In the intervention group, an ultrasound-guided nerve block was performed after spinal anaesthesia using a high-frequency linear probe and an in-plane needle approach, with ropivacaine injected around the target nerve under direct vision. Spread of local anaesthetic around the nerve was confirmed on the ultrasound image. Blocks were performed by consultant anaesthetists or by senior trainees under direct supervision, all of whom had completed the departmental training programme in ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia.
Postoperative analgesia in both groups followed the same written multimodal regimen of regular paracetamol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug unless contraindicated, and oral rescue medication on request. Ward staff were asked not to change the regimen for the purposes of the trial.
2.5 Outcomes. The primary outcome was pain at rest 24 hours after the end of surgery, measured on an 11-point numerical rating scale from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable) by a blinded assessor. Secondary outcomes were pain on movement at 24 hours, rescue medication use, time to first mobilisation with a physiotherapist, patient satisfaction with analgesia at 48 hours, postoperative nausea and vomiting, block-related complications, falls during the hospital stay, and the length of stay. A prespecified sensitivity analysis examined opioid consumption after excluding patients with prior opioid use, defined as any regular opioid prescription in the three months before surgery.
2.6 Sample size. Based on pilot data from our unit and a minimal clinically important difference on the numerical rating scale, we estimated that 72 patients per group would provide 90 percent power at a two-sided significance level of 0.05. Allowing for losses to follow-up, we planned to randomise 160 patients.
2.7 Statistical analysis. The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle. Continuous outcomes were compared using linear regression adjusted for the stratification factor, and binary outcomes using logistic regression. Time to first mobilisation was analysed using survival methods, with patients discharged before mobilisation censored. Missing primary outcome data were handled by multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption, with a complete-case analysis reported alongside. No interim analysis was planned. Analyses were performed with standard statistical software by a statistician blinded to allocation.
2.8 Data collection and management. Trial data were recorded on paper case report forms by research nurses and transcribed into a secure database with range and consistency checks. A second member of the research team checked a random sample of forms against the source documents. Pain scores for the trial were recorded by assessors who had not been present in the block room and who did not have access to the anaesthetic chart. Physiotherapists recorded the time of first mobilisation on a standard form, and the length of stay was taken from the hospital administrative system.
2.9 Patient and public involvement. Two patients who had previously undergone knee replacement in our unit reviewed the protocol and the patient information sheet. They advised that pain on the first full day after surgery, rather than in the recovery room, was the period they remembered as most difficult, which supported our choice of primary time point. They also asked that the information sheet explain clearly that the block might cause temporary numbness of the leg, and this was added before recruitment began.
2.10 Trial oversight. A trial management group met monthly during recruitment to review progress, protocol adherence and adverse events. Because the interventions were in routine clinical use and the trial was small, a separate data monitoring committee was not convened; serious adverse events were reported to the ethics committee as required.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text: 3.1 Participant flow and baseline characteristics. Between the start of recruitment and its planned end, 214 patients were screened, of whom 160 were randomised: 80 to the nerve-block group and 80 to the control group. The commonest reasons for exclusion were declining to take part and planned general anaesthesia. All randomised patients received the allocated intervention and were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. The groups were well balanced at baseline (Table 1).

table.caption: Table 1. Baseline characteristics of randomised patients

sections.heading: 3.2 Primary outcome
sections.text: Pain at rest was recorded at 24 hours for all patients by the blinded assessor. The mean pain score at 24 hours was 3.1 with the block and 5.2 without (p < 0.001). The difference exceeded the minimal clinically important difference set out in the protocol, and the complete-case and imputed analyses gave the same conclusion.

table.caption: Table 2. Primary outcome: pain at rest 24 hours after surgery (0-10 numerical rating scale)

sections.heading: 3.3 Secondary outcomes
sections.text:
Pain on movement at 24 hours was lower in the nerve-block group, in the same direction as the primary outcome. Patients in the nerve-block group mobilised with the physiotherapist earlier on average, and more of them reported being satisfied or very satisfied with their pain relief at 48 hours. The length of stay did not differ meaningfully between the groups, which we attribute partly to discharge being scheduled by day of the week rather than by readiness during the trial period.
Postoperative nausea and vomiting occurred at similar rates in the two groups. No falls were recorded in either group during the hospital stay. One patient in the nerve-block group reported transient numbness of the medial calf that resolved before the six-week clinic review; no vascular puncture, local anaesthetic toxicity or persistent nerve injury occurred (Table 3).

table.caption: Table 3. Adverse events during the hospital stay

figure.caption: Figure 2. Pain at rest over the first 48 hours by group (numerical rating scale, mean and 95 percent confidence interval).

sections.heading: 3.4 Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: The prespecified sensitivity analysis excluded patients with prior opioid use, so that opioid consumption could be described in patients who were opioid-naive before surgery. In the sensitivity analysis excluding patients with prior opioid use, the mean opioid dose in the nerve-block group was 12 mg. This analysis was descriptive and was not powered for formal comparison.

table.caption: Table 4. Sensitivity analysis excluding patients with prior opioid use

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In this randomised trial in patients undergoing primary total knee replacement, adding an ultrasound-guided nerve block to a standard multimodal regimen reduced pain at rest 24 hours after surgery by a clinically important margin. The benefit was achieved without an increase in falls or serious block-related complications, and was accompanied by earlier mobilisation and greater patient satisfaction.
Our choice of 24 hours as the primary time point was deliberate. Pain in the first few hours after knee replacement is strongly influenced by the residual effect of spinal anaesthesia and by local infiltration, so differences measured early may say little about the period in which patients are expected to stand, walk and begin exercises. By 24 hours, these early effects have largely faded, and the remaining difference between groups is more likely to reflect the contribution of the block itself.
The findings are consistent with the rationale for motor-sparing approaches. Because the block was placed under direct ultrasound vision and targeted predominantly sensory branches, quadriceps function appeared to be preserved well enough for physiotherapy to start early, and no falls occurred. We did not measure quadriceps strength formally, and future trials should include an objective measure of motor function alongside pain.
The pragmatic design is a strength. The trial was conducted on a routine elective list by the anaesthetists who normally provide the service, and the multimodal regimen was the one in daily use on the ward. The results are therefore likely to apply to similar units that already offer ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia. Units without that expertise would need to account for training time and equipment before adopting the technique.
The lack of a meaningful difference in length of stay deserves comment. During the trial, discharge after knee replacement in our hospital was organised around fixed physiotherapy and pharmacy schedules rather than individual readiness, and many patients who were clinically ready waited for these services. Better pain control is a necessary but not sufficient condition for earlier discharge; pathway redesign is also needed.
4.1 Limitations. The trial has several limitations. It was conducted at a single centre, which may limit generalisability. Patients and the treating anaesthetist were not blinded because no sham block was used; we judged that a sham injection carried risk without benefit to the patient, and we mitigated bias by blinding outcome assessors and ward staff recording trial data. The secondary outcomes and the sensitivity analysis were not powered for formal inference and should be read as supportive. Finally, follow-up ended at six weeks, so we cannot comment on any effect of the block on longer-term function or on the development of persistent postsurgical pain.
4.2 Comparison with other approaches. Several alternatives to a peripheral nerve block are in use for knee replacement. Periarticular infiltration by the surgeon is simple, requires no additional equipment and was given to every patient in this trial, so our results describe the added value of a block over and above infiltration rather than a comparison between the two. Continuous catheter techniques can extend the duration of analgesia but add complexity, the risk of catheter displacement, and the need for pump management on the ward. Intrathecal additives can prolong analgesia after spinal anaesthesia but bring their own side effects, including pruritus and urinary retention. A single-shot ultrasound-guided block occupies a middle ground: it adds a few minutes in the block room, requires skills that are now widely taught, and in our trial was not associated with additional harm.
The relative merits of these approaches are likely to depend on the setting. In a unit with established ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia and a block room that runs in parallel with the operating theatre, the extra time is small. In a unit where the block would delay the start of surgery, or where few anaesthetists are trained, infiltration alone may remain the pragmatic choice. Trials comparing combinations of these techniques directly, with attention to both analgesia and motor function, would help units choose.
4.3 Implications for practice and research. For units that already deliver ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia, these results support offering a nerve block to patients undergoing total knee replacement as part of a multimodal pathway. Future work should test the technique in day-case pathways, in older and frailer patients, and in combination with structured early discharge, and should measure motor function directly.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text: An ultrasound-guided nerve block added to standard multimodal analgesia reduced pain 24 hours after primary total knee replacement, with a favourable safety profile and earlier mobilisation. It is a useful component of analgesic pathways for knee replacement in units with the necessary expertise.

sections.heading: Funding and conflicts of interest
sections.text: The trial was funded by a departmental research grant. The funder had no role in the design, conduct, analysis or reporting of the trial. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Anonymised data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

documents.text:
Correction to: Ultrasound-guided nerve block and pain after knee surgery

In Table 4 (the sensitivity analysis excluding patients with prior opioid use), the mean opioid dose in the nerve-block group was reported as 12 mg and should read 19 mg. The primary outcome in Table 2 and all other results are unchanged.

draft_doc.title: Regional anaesthesia in day-case orthopaedics
draft_doc.authors: Hartley, S., Achterberg, M., Kamau, J. Day Surgery Research Group, Fake University School of Medicine
draft_doc.abstract: Day-case pathways for joint replacement promise shorter stays, lower costs and a quicker return home, but they depend on analgesia that is effective, safe and compatible with early walking. This draft sets out the background and design of a planned trial of regional anaesthesia in patients having knee replacement on a same-day discharge pathway. We review what is known about patient selection, analgesia, mobilisation and discharge in ambulatory orthopaedics, describe the evidence that motivates our primary outcome, and outline the trial's methods, outcomes and analysis.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Over the last decade, orthopaedic surgery has moved steadily towards the day-case model. Procedures that once required several nights in hospital, such as anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and shoulder arthroscopy, are now routinely performed with discharge on the same day, and units in several health systems have begun to offer same-day discharge after hip and knee replacement to selected patients [1, 21]. The appeal is clear: shorter stays free beds for other patients, reduce the costs associated with an overnight admission [11], and are preferred by many patients who would rather recover at home [4].
The move to day-case joint replacement nonetheless raises practical questions. Patients must be able to walk safely, manage stairs where needed, pass urine, tolerate oral intake and have adequate pain control before they leave. Each of these discharge criteria [6] can be undermined by the anaesthetic and analgesic plan. Spinal anaesthesia with long-acting agents can delay mobilisation and urinary function [9], systemic opioids cause nausea, drowsiness and constipation [16], and blocks that weaken the quadriceps raise the risk of falls [7].
Patient selection is a second challenge. Early day-case programmes enrolled younger, fitter patients with few comorbidities [21], and readmission rates in those cohorts were reassuringly low [10]. As programmes expand, they increasingly include older patients and those with frailty [13, 22], in whom the balance between analgesia, mobility and safety may differ. Evidence from inpatient pathways may not transfer directly to these groups, or to a setting in which the first night after surgery is spent at home without nursing observation [20].
Analgesia is therefore central to whether a day-case pathway succeeds. Pain that is tolerable on the ward with nursing support may become a reason for an emergency call or readmission once the patient is home. Regional techniques that provide prolonged analgesia without motor block are attractive for this reason, and they fit naturally within multimodal pathways that already combine regular simple analgesics and local infiltration [8]. Yet the ambulatory setting brings its own concerns, including rebound pain as a block wears off during the first night [19] and the need for clear information so that patients know what to expect and when to seek help [23].
In this draft we first review the evidence that motivates our trial, then describe how we will test an ultrasound-guided nerve block in a day-case population, and finally set out the outcomes and analysis plan. Our aim is to establish whether a technique shown to work on inpatient wards delivers the same benefit when patients go home on the day of surgery.

sections.heading: 1.1 Current practice in the participating units
sections.text:
The three units that will take part in the trial have each run a day-case knee replacement pathway for at least two years. Patients are identified at the surgical clinic and seen at a dedicated preoperative assessment visit, where a nurse specialist confirms that they meet the day-case criteria, explains the pathway, and checks that a responsible adult will be at home for the first night. Surgery is scheduled as the first or second case on a morning list so that there is time for mobilisation and discharge assessment in the afternoon.
The anaesthetic approach varies between units and between anaesthetists. All three units use spinal anaesthesia as the default, but the choice of agent, the use of sedation and the use of peripheral nerve blocks differ. In one unit, most patients receive a nerve block; in the other two, blocks are used at the discretion of the anaesthetist on the day. Local infiltration analgesia by the surgeon is routine in all three units. Each unit has a written multimodal analgesic regimen for the ward and for discharge, and each provides a telephone number that patients can call overnight.
Audits in the participating units suggest that the most common reasons for a planned day-case patient staying overnight are pain, dizziness on standing, nausea and delayed return of urinary function, with pain the single most frequent. Patients who go home as planned and later call the unit most often do so during the first night or the following morning, again most commonly because of pain. These observations shaped our choice of primary outcome and of the time at which it is measured.
This variation in practice is itself a reason for a trial. Where a technique is used by some anaesthetists and not by others, without good evidence for either choice, a randomised comparison embedded in routine care is both ethical and informative [18]. Our anaesthetic colleagues in the three units have agreed to the protocol and to the randomisation of their patients.

sections.heading: 2. Background and rationale
sections.text:
Peripheral nerve blocks for knee surgery have evolved from the femoral nerve block, which gives reliable analgesia at the cost of quadriceps weakness [3], to more distal approaches that target predominantly sensory branches [12]. Ultrasound guidance has made these blocks more reliable and easier to teach [5], and it is now standard practice in many units.
Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks lower pain at 24 hours after knee replacement (Oyelaran et al. [15]: 3.1 versus 5.2), the outcome we test in a new population. That inpatient trial chose 24 hours deliberately, as the point at which spinal anaesthesia has worn off and mobilisation has begun, and the same time point matters even more on a day-case pathway: by 24 hours a day-case patient has spent the first night at home, and pain at that point is the outcome most likely to drive telephone calls, unplanned attendances and dissatisfaction.
Whether the inpatient result holds after same-day discharge is not known. Patients on day-case pathways differ from inpatients in ways that may matter. They are selected for fitness, but they also lose the nursing observation, rescue analgesia on request and physiotherapy contact that an inpatient receives during the first night. The block may therefore matter more in this setting, if it substitutes for support that is no longer available, or less, if rebound pain at home erodes its benefit [19]. Quadriceps strength is also of particular concern at home, where a fall may happen without anyone present [2, 7].
Pain measurement brings its own considerations. The 11-point numerical rating scale is well validated and easily used by patients at home [14], and it allows direct comparison with the inpatient trial that motivates our study. Remote collection of pain scores by telephone or a mobile application is feasible in ambulatory surgery [20], although the context of measurement differs from a bedside assessment by a blinded researcher.
Finally, pragmatic trials embedded in routine services are increasingly favoured in anaesthesia because they answer questions about effectiveness rather than efficacy [18]. A day-case pathway is a natural setting for such a design: the population, the anaesthetic team and the discharge process are those that would apply if the technique were adopted.

sections.heading: 3. Planned methods
sections.text:
3.1 Design. We plan a multicentre, pragmatic, randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment, comparing an ultrasound-guided nerve block plus standard day-case multimodal analgesia with standard day-case multimodal analgesia alone, in adults having primary unilateral knee replacement on a same-day discharge pathway.
3.2 Participants. Eligible patients will be adults listed for primary knee replacement who meet the participating units' criteria for day-case surgery, including a responsible adult at home for the first night and access to a telephone. We will deliberately include patients aged 75 years and older, and we will record frailty using a validated scale [22], so that results can be reported for the older patients increasingly offered day-case surgery [13].
3.3 Interventions. All patients will receive spinal anaesthesia with a short-acting agent chosen to support same-day mobilisation [9], local infiltration analgesia by the surgeon, and the unit's written multimodal regimen of regular simple analgesics. In the intervention group, an ultrasound-guided motor-sparing nerve block will be performed by anaesthetists trained in the technique. Patients in both groups will receive the same written discharge information, including advice about the expected wearing off of the block and the use of their take-home analgesia [23].
3.4 Outcomes. The primary outcome will be pain at rest 24 hours after surgery on the 11-point numerical rating scale, collected by a researcher unaware of allocation by telephone. Secondary outcomes will include pain on movement at 24 hours, successful same-day discharge, unplanned contact with health services in the first seven days, readmission within 30 days [10], falls, patient-reported quality of recovery [4], and postoperative nausea and vomiting [16].
3.5 Sample size. The sample size will be based on the minimal clinically important difference on the numerical rating scale [17], with allowance for loss to follow-up and for clustering by centre. We will finalise the calculation once pilot data on the variance of 24-hour pain scores collected by telephone are available.
3.6 Analysis. The primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat principle using a mixed-effects model with centre as a random effect. A prespecified subgroup analysis will examine patients aged 75 years and older. A cost analysis will compare the resources used in each group, including unplanned contacts and readmissions [11].

sections.heading: 4. Expected contribution
sections.text:
If the benefit of an ultrasound-guided nerve block seen on inpatient wards is confirmed in a day-case population, the trial will provide direct evidence to support including the block in same-day discharge pathways for knee replacement. If it is not, the trial will show where the inpatient evidence does not transfer and will guide alternative strategies, such as extended local infiltration or structured remote follow-up. In either case, by including older and frailer patients and by collecting outcomes after the patient has gone home, the trial addresses gaps that inpatient studies cannot fill.
We also expect the trial to inform service design. The feasibility of collecting pain scores remotely, the proportion of patients who achieve same-day discharge, and the pattern of unplanned contacts in the first week will all be useful to units planning to expand their day-case orthopaedic programmes [1, 6].

sections.heading: 5. Ethics and dissemination
sections.text: The protocol will be submitted to the relevant research ethics committees before recruitment begins. Patients will give written informed consent at the preoperative assessment visit, and they will be told that they can withdraw at any time without affecting their care. Results will be submitted for publication regardless of their direction, and a plain-language summary will be sent to participants.

expected.why: Rubric: a correction to a secondary number is low; 'affected' is no when the change is elsewhere (Table 4, not Table 2), and impact is none when no use is affected. The draft is strong key_evidence and the alert_severity from the rules is medium, so overreacting is tempting.
